title: Visualizing the CLT — Shape of \(\bar{x}\) as \(n\) Grows

steps.instruction: The **Population** panel shows a strongly **right-skewed** population. In Class Example 6.2 you saw that \(\bar{x}\) is always centered at \(\mu\) — now we watch its **shape**. The **Central Limit Theorem** claims that as the sample size \(n\) grows, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) becomes **normal (bell-shaped)** *even when the population is skewed*. The tool is set to \(n = 5\).
steps.observe: Right now \(n = 5\) is tiny. Keep your eye on the **shape** of the bottom panel as we push \(n\) up.

steps.instruction: **Before drawing, commit to a prediction.** You'll build the sampling distribution at \(n=5\), then \(n=30\), then \(n=100\), all drawn from this same skewed population.

gate.question: As \(n\) increases from 5 to 100, what happens to the **shape** of the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\)?

choices.text: It gradually becomes symmetric and bell-shaped
It stays just as right-skewed as the population — the skew never leaves
It flattens out — every mean becomes equally likely

gate.feedback: You've committed — now draw all three sample sizes and watch whether the shape changes.

steps.instruction: Tick **Show normal curve**, then click **+1000** to draw about a thousand sample means at \(n = 5\).

requires.hint: Click **+1000** to draw at least 500 sample means at \(n=5\), then continue.

steps.observe: At \(n=5\), the sampling distribution is still noticeably **right-skewed** — it doesn't hug the normal curve.
steps.reveal: Averaging just **5** values isn't enough to wash out a strong skew, so the population's shape still shows through. Small \(n\) — the CLT hasn't kicked in yet.

steps.instruction: Now set **Sample size \(n\)** to **30** (this clears the plot) and click **+1000**.

requires.hint: Set **\(n = 30\)**, then click **+1000** to fill the new distribution.

steps.observe: The skew has largely straightened out — the pile is much more symmetric and now tracks the normal curve fairly well.

steps.instruction: Set **\(n\)** to **100** (clears the plot) and click **+1000** once more.
steps.observe: Now it's a clean, symmetric **bell** sitting right on the normal curve.

gate.question: Which sample size would you trust to give a bell-shaped sampling distribution for this skewed population?

choices.text: No \(n\) works — a skewed population never gives a normal \(\bar{x}\)

gate.feedback: By \(n=30\) the skew is mostly gone, and by \(n=100\) it's a clean bell — that's the CLT at work. This is exactly where the **\(n > 30\)** rule of thumb for means comes from.
gate.retryFeedback: Compare the three shapes you drew: \(n=5\) was skewed, but from \(n=30\) on it looked bell-shaped.

steps.instruction: One more comparison. Switch the **Population shape** to **Normal**, set **\(n\)** back to **5**, and click **+1000**.

requires.hint: Choose the **Normal** population shape, set **\(n = 5\)**, then click **+1000**.

steps.observe: With a **normal** population, even \(n=5\) gives a clean bell — no large sample needed.

prompts.label: Why did the skewed population need a large \(n\) before \(\bar{x}\) looked normal, while the normal population didn't?

respond.answer: For a **skewed** population, small samples inherit the skew — it takes a larger \(n\) (here about 30) for averaging to smooth the sampling distribution into a bell. For a population that's **already normal**, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) is normal at *every* \(n\), even \(n=5\). The \(n>30\) rule of thumb is insurance against skew — you need it only when the population isn't already bell-shaped.

steps.reveal: The **Central Limit Theorem**: whatever the population's shape, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) becomes approximately **normal** once \(n\) is large enough — and the more skewed the population, the larger the \(n\) you need. A roughly normal population is normal at any \(n\); a strongly skewed one needs \(n\) around 30 or more. This is why we can use normal-based inference for means once the sample is large enough, even without a normal population.
